claims.text: An integrated machine-learning surrogate augmented with DFT and MD/BTE constraints will predict the decoupled lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr with less than 10% error.
The model can isolate oxygen-induced phonon scattering effects from electronic heat transport.
Pre-2024 experimental and simulation datasets characterize both pristine, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Phonon density of states, elastic constants, scattering rates, and experimental thermal-conductivity measurements provide suitable inputs for training the proposed model.
Physics-based constraints can enforce correct temperature dependence and anharmonic phonon behavior in the model.
Lattice conduction is prominent at approximately 50 K in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen affects phonon transport through local force-constant variations represented by oxygen-content descriptors and vibrational features.
Independent surrogate functions for phonon and electronic conductivity will decouple the two heat-transport channels.
Conservation constraints and expected anharmonic temperature dependencies will keep the model physically sound and prevent overfitting.
Adding 1 wt.% oxygen will reduce lattice thermal conductivity by approximately 30% at high temperatures because of oxygen-induced phonon scattering.
The model will capture a crossover near 200 K at which electronic heat transport becomes comparable to lattice heat transport.
Current approaches use either simplified Debye models or defect-free simulations.
Current approaches conflate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
Prior analytical approaches typically have predictive errors exceeding 20–30%.
The model is applicable from 50 to 1200 K and should not be extrapolated to substantially different impurity concentrations or temperatures outside that interval.
Phonon spectroscopy and Hall-effect measurements can provide separate lattice and electronic contributions adequate for testing the model.

contradictions.description: The initial-state and conditions fields state that the model applies to both pristine and 1 wt.% oxygen samples, whereas the boundary field describes applicability only for samples with oxygen content around 1 wt.%, apparently excluding the pristine control.
